text: The Lucasian Chair of Mathematics (/luːˈkeɪziən/) is a mathematics professorship at the University of Cambridge, England, with its holder known as the Lucasian Professor. The post was founded in 1663 by Henry Lucas, who served as Cambridge University's Member of Parliament from 1639 to 1640, and was officially established by King Charles II on 18 January 1664. It is regarded as the most celebrated and prestigious professorship in the world, recognized for the distinguished achievements of its holders and their groundbreaking contributions, with The Daily Telegraph describing it as one of the most prestigious academic posts globally.[1][2] Henry Lucas bequeathed his library of 4,000 volumes to the university and specified the purchase of land that would yield £100 annually to fund the professorship.[3] It is the third oldest mathematics chair in Great Britain, following the Gresham Professor of Geometry at Gresham College and the Savilian Professor of Geometry at the University of Oxford.[4] During the 1800s and subsequent decades, Lucasian professors played key roles in establishing Britain as the leading scientific nation and in transforming the university from a ‘gentleman’s club’ into a research institution.[5] Babbage applied for the vacancy in 1826 after Turton, but Airy was appointed; William Whewell, who considered applying but preferred both Herschel and Babbage, stated he would have been the best professor, though college heads did not see it. Babbage was eventually appointed when the chair became available two years later.[6] Michael Cates is the current Lucasian Professor, beginning on 1 July 2015.[7] The University of Cambridge now requires Lucasian Chair holders to retire at age 67, as was the case with Stephen Hawking.[8] In the final episode of the science-fiction series Star Trek: The Next Generation, the android Data holds the Lucasian Chair in the late 24th century, though in an alternate reality.[9][10][11]
